power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: "Borderline" is likely an "identity" or "emotional" disorder, but definitely not a "personality" disorder: A commentary on Sharp et al. (2026)

author.affiliation:
University College London
								Unit of Psychoanalysis

text.text: In a 17-year longitudinal study, Sharp et al. (2026)  report that "self-functioning" outperforms "interpersonal functioning" in predicting later borderline pathology, concluding that the core and distinguishing features of "personality disorder" lie in the "representation of self".
In this commentary, I suggest that these findings can be interpreted in at least two alternative ways.

First, I argue that when we take the authors' findings at face value, we reach the conclusion that (borderline) personality disorder can be understood as an "identity disorder" given that its main impairments lie in "the representation of self".

Second, I argue that when examined closely, the authors' findings suggest that "(borderline) personality disorder" is an "emotional disorder", given that the predictor of "self-functioning" is constructed with items that encode emotional, not self-related, pathology.
Finally, I conclude by noting that whichever way Sharp et al.'s findings are interpreted, they cannot support the inference that "(borderline) personality disorder" is in any way about "personality".
I recently had the pleasure of reading Sharp et al.'s (2025) study on developmental trajectories of self-and interpersonal functioning in relation to subsequent borderline pathology.
text.formatted: I recently had the pleasure of reading <ref type="bibr">Sharp et al.'s (2025)</ref> study on developmental trajectories of self-and interpersonal functioning in relation to subsequent borderline pathology.

text.text: The authors analysed a rich longitudinal dataset of childhood -adolescent mental health problems, showing that what they term "self-functioning" outcompeted "interpersonal-functioning" in the 17-year prospective prediction of later borderline psychopathology.
On that basis, Sharp et al. (2025, p.20), then, concluded that "the core and distinguishing features of personality disorder lie […] the representation of self".
text.formatted: On that basis, <ref type="bibr">Sharp et al. (2025, p.20)</ref>, then, concluded that "the core and distinguishing features of personality disorder lie <ref type="bibr">[…]</ref> the representation of self".

text.text: In this commentary, I suggest that these findings can be interpreted in at least two additional ways, which I feel were unacknowledged by Sharp and colleagues.
To begin with, when we take the authors' findings at face value, we can conclude that they imply that "borderline personality disorder" may actually be an "identity disorder."

To appreciate this inference, consider the case of "multiple personality disorder" which was re-conceptualised as "dissociative identity disorder" when its primary impairments were appreciate to include the "dissociation" of various "identities" (not personalities; see Cardeña et al., 1996, p.875).
text.formatted: To appreciate this inference, consider the case of "multiple personality disorder" which was re-conceptualised as "dissociative identity disorder" when its primary impairments were appreciate to include the "dissociation" of various "identities" (not personalities; see <ref type="bibr">Cardeña et al., 1996, p.875)</ref>.

text.text: In the same exact way, if we accept Sharp et al.'s conclusion that "the core and distinguishing features of personality disorder lie […] the representation of self", then we must also accept the next logical inference, which is that this pathology is fundamentally about identity, not about personality. 1Importantly, while Sharp and colleagues (2025) may object to this reinterpretation of their findings, it is worth noting that their discussion half-embraces the aforementioned logic.
text.formatted: In the same exact way, if we accept Sharp et al.'s conclusion that "the core and distinguishing features of personality disorder lie […] the representation of self", then we must also accept the next logical inference, which is that this pathology is fundamentally about identity, not about personality. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref>Importantly, while Sharp and colleagues (2025) may object to this reinterpretation of their findings, it is worth noting that their discussion half-embraces the aforementioned logic.

text.text: Indeed, in their discussion, Sharp et al. (2025, p.19) leverage the asymmetric prediction of self-versus interpersonal-functioning to reject the re-labelling of personality disorder as "interpersonal disorder" by stating that: "with regard to approaches that promote the renaming of personality disorder as interpersonal disorders, our findings suggest that such renaming would diminish the role of the aspect of personality functioning that denotes 'personhood'".
text.formatted: Indeed, in their discussion, <ref type="bibr">Sharp et al. (2025, p.19</ref>) leverage the asymmetric prediction of self-versus interpersonal-functioning to reject the re-labelling of personality disorder as "interpersonal disorder" by stating that: "with regard to approaches that promote the renaming of personality disorder as interpersonal disorders, our findings suggest that such renaming would diminish the role of the aspect of personality functioning that denotes 'personhood'".

text.text: In doing so, however, Sharp et al. essentially make the same argument I made above in reverse: that is, they use primary predictive effects (i.e., self-functioning > interpersonal functioning) to reject a label centred on interpersonal dysfunction and embrace an alternative label centred on self-representation.
text.formatted: In doing so, however, Sharp et al. essentially make the same argument I made above in reverse: that is, they use primary predictive effects (i.e., self-functioning > interpersonal functioning) to reject a label centred on interpersonal dysfunction and embrace an alternative label centred on self-representation.

text.text: What the authors do not also do, however, is complete this half-inference by drawing the appropriate conclusion, which is that: if personality disorder's pathology lies in "self-functioning" (or identity), then by definition this is an self-functioning (or identity) pathology, rather than a general personality pathology.
1  Second, beyond this first re-interpretation of Sharp et al.'s findings, there is reason to suspect that there is another interpretation of the authors' findings.

Indeed, when we look more closely at how the authors operationalised their predictor "self-functioning", we begin to suspect that the authors' findings may speak less to "the representation of self" and more to other psychopathology problems (specifically, emotional problems).

To illustrate the logic behind this re-interpretation more concretely, I will rely on a simple exercise of face validity: specifically, I will look closely at each item employed by the authors to construct their predictor "self-functioning" (Table 1) and I will ask myself the following simple question: what does this item appear to measure?
text.formatted: To illustrate the logic behind this re-interpretation more concretely, I will rely on a simple exercise of face validity: specifically, I will look closely at each item employed by the authors to construct their predictor "self-functioning" (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>) and I will ask myself the following simple question: what does this item appear to measure?

text.text: Doing this for all 14 items used by the authors to operationalise their so-called measure of "selffunctioning", I believe we can find at least four different sets of items.

The first set includes 4 out of 14 items, which appear to reflect diagnostic symptoms of "major depression", as defined in the DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022), including worthlessness ("self-depreciation and self-hatred"), excessive guilt ("pathological guilt"), thoughts of death ("thinking about death"), and anhedonia ("loss of affect").

The second set includes 6 out of 14 items, which appear to reflect broader indicators of emotional psychopathology (or what was historically known as "neurosis", rather than "borderline" or "psychosis"), including self-pitying ("feeling sorry for oneself"), depressive cognition ("hopelessness" and "helplessness"), "boredom", and irritable mood ("touchy or easily annoyed", "angry or resentful").

The third set includes 2 of the 14 items, which appear to paradoxically reflect interpersonal-emotional psychopathology, rather than self-pathology per se, in the sense that they capture affective states with explicit interpersonal reference, namely, the feeling of "being alone or friendless" and a "feeling of being unloved or uncared for by others".

Finally, only the last set which includes 2 of the 14 items could be plausibly defended as reflecting AMPD-defined self-functioning, in the sense that these two items index self-related pathology most commonly associated with narcissistic personality, including "grandiosity" and "bragging" (APA, 2022).
Self-depreciation and self-hatred An unjustified feeling of inferiority to others (including unjustified feelings of ugliness).
Self-hatred involves severe hostility directed by the child against him/herself, accompanied by expressed dislike or expressed criticism.
Major depression (worthlessness criterion), but see note below.
Pathological guilt Excessive self-blame for minor or nonexistent wrongdoings.
Child realizes that guilt is exaggerated.
Thinking about death Thoughts about death and dying, whether referred to self or others.
Include thoughts about not being able to go on any longer and life not being worth living.
Include discussion about a grandparent who has died ("Do they go to heaven?"
"What will happen when I die?").
Major depression (recurrent thoughts of death criterion)
Loss of affect Complaint of loss of a previously existing ability to feel or experience emotion.
Feeling sorry for oneself A feeling that life or people have been unfairly unpleasant or troubling and that the child deserves better.
Child feels unlucky, victim of "bad luck".
Emotional psychopathology (selfpitying cognition; but also partly interpersonal in content)
The child has a bleak, negative, pessimistic view of the future, and little hope that his/her situation will improve.
This is a generalized feeling.
Emotional psychopathology (depressive cognition)
The child feels that there is little or nothing s/he can do to improve his/her situation or psychological state, though such a change would be welcome.
This is a generalized feeling.

Emotional psychopathology (depressive cognition) Boredom Activities the child is actually engaged in are felt to be dull and lacking in interest while interest in other possible potential activities is expressed.
Emotional psychopathology (dysphoric restlessness / under-stimulation)
Touchy or easily annoyed The child is generally more prone to feelings of anger, bad temper, short temper, resentment, sulking or annoyance, under minor provocation than most children.
Angry or resentful The child is generally more prone to manifestations of anger or resentment (such as snappiness, shouting, quarreling or sulking) under minor provocation, than most children.
Loneliness A feeling of being alone and/or friendless, regardless of the justification for the feeling; total daily duration of at least 1hour.
Feels unloved A generalized feeling of being unloved and uncared for, regardless of the justification for that feeling.
Interpersonal-emotional psychopathology (feeling unloved/uncared for by others)

An unusually increased level of self-esteem or self-appraisal of worth, such as the feeling of being superbly strong, or exceptionally able, or intelligent, when in expansive or expansive/irritable mood or irritable mood.
Narcissistic kind of self-pathology (inflated self-esteem)
Bragging Boastful talking about his/her real or perceived talents, accomplishments, etc.
Narcissistic kind of self-pathology (boastful talk directed at others)
Note1.
The authors' items were drawn from the Preschool Age Psychiatric Assessment (PAPA; Egger & Angold, 2004) and the Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Assessment (CAPA; Angold & Costello, 2000).
text.formatted: The authors' items were drawn from the Preschool Age Psychiatric Assessment (PAPA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Egger & Angold, 2004)</ref> and the Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Assessment (CAPA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Angold & Costello, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Note2.
The item "Self-depreciation and self-hatred" could be argued to reflect self-pathology on the grounds that the self-hatred component captures a form of maladaptive selfrelating.
However, both the AMPD and the broader psychodynamic tradition reserve this designation for more severe enactments of self-attack (e.g., non-suicidal self-injury, self-harm).
Self-hatred expressed only at the cognitive-affective level remains a fundamentally neurotic phenomenon and is captured by the worthlessness criterion of major depression (APA, 2022).

Looking at this list of indicators, I ask myself and the readers as well: Is the main theme reflected by these items genuinely self-related pathology (or even personality-related pathology) or is it perhaps something more specific like "emotional pathology" (most commonly associated with depression, as a diagnostic category).

Unless I am misreading every single one of these items, then the answer is most likely the latter: that is, most of these items (specifically 12 out of 14 items) appear to reflect emotional problems in the sense that they deal with ways of feeling, not ways of re-presenting oneself (as Carla et al. imply in p.20).
text.formatted: Unless I am misreading every single one of these items, then the answer is most likely the latter: that is, most of these items (specifically 12 out of 14 items) appear to reflect emotional problems in the sense that they deal with ways of feeling, not ways of re-presenting oneself <ref type="bibr">(as Carla et al. imply in p.20)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, what the authors call a measure of "selffunctioning", when closely examined, appears to reflect "emotional functioning".

Importantly, then, what the authors interpret as evidence for "personhood" or "selffunctioning" being central to borderline psychopathology can now be appreciated to be evidence for "emotional pathology" being central to borderline psychopathology.

And, interestingly, this re-interpretation of Sharp et al.'s (2025) findings is remarkably consistent with a longstanding line of work that has viewed borderline personality disorder as fundamentally an emotional disorder rather than a personality disorder.
text.formatted: And, interestingly, this re-interpretation of <ref type="bibr">Sharp et al.'s (2025)</ref> findings is remarkably consistent with a longstanding line of work that has viewed borderline personality disorder as fundamentally an emotional disorder rather than a personality disorder.

text.text: Specifically, at the empirical level, a systematic review of 39 prospective longitudinal studies found childhood and adolescent internalising symptoms (such as depression, anxiety) as one of the most consistently replicated predictors of subsequent borderline pathology, concluding that this developmental risk profile is indistinguishable from that of internalising disorders more broadly (Stepp et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Specifically, at the empirical level, a systematic review of 39 prospective longitudinal studies found childhood and adolescent internalising symptoms (such as depression, anxiety) as one of the most consistently replicated predictors of subsequent borderline pathology, concluding that this developmental risk profile is indistinguishable from that of internalising disorders more broadly <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Stepp et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, at the theoretical level, several theorists have independently argued that borderline personality disorder may neither be "borderline" nor a "personality pathology" (Tyrer, 2009) because it can be instead re-interpreted as an "emotional disorder" given that most of its impairments (indicating instability across ways of thinking, feeling, and behaving) are fundamentally aspects of emotional pathology (e.g., see Linehan, 1993; Sauer-Zavala & Barlow, 2014).
text.formatted: Likewise, at the theoretical level, several theorists have independently argued that borderline personality disorder may neither be "borderline" nor a "personality pathology" <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Tyrer, 2009)</ref> because it can be instead re-interpreted as an "emotional disorder" given that most of its impairments (indicating instability across ways of thinking, feeling, and behaving) are fundamentally aspects of emotional pathology (e.g., see <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Linehan, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Sauer-Zavala & Barlow, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, and most recently, at the lived experience level, general psychiatric patients have themselves indicated a preference for the label "emotional intensity disorder" over "borderline personality disorder", implying that the most relevant stakeholders (namely, the patients themselves) agree that borderline problems are fundamentally about "ways of feeling" rather than "personality" or even "identity" (see Hayward et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Finally, and most recently, at the lived experience level, general psychiatric patients have themselves indicated a preference for the label "emotional intensity disorder" over "borderline personality disorder", implying that the most relevant stakeholders (namely, the patients themselves) agree that borderline problems are fundamentally about "ways of feeling" rather than "personality" or even "identity" (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Hayward et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Viewed alongside these findings, then, the study by Sharp and colleagues 2 It is important to note that this re-interpretation (i.e., the authors' self-functioning being emotional functioning, instead) is not ruled out by the authors' adjustment for "internalizing symptoms" because Sarp et al.'s (2025, p.14) internalizing covariate includes anxiety and post-traumatic stress symptoms but not depressive symptoms (which, as outlined in Table 1, are the main emotional symptoms captured by the authors' construct of "self-functioning").

In essence, then, what the authors' analyses show is that depressive symptoms (or what the authors call "self-functioning") predicts subsequent borderline pathology beyond anxiety and post-traumatic stress (or what the authors call "internalising").
appears to provide one of the strongest pieces of evidence to date in support of the reconceptualisation of borderline personality disorder as an emotional disorder.
3   To summarise, then, the study by Sharp and colleagues (2025) raises at least two important take-home messages, depending on how its findings are interpreted.
text.formatted: 3   To summarise, then, the study by <ref type="bibr">Sharp and colleagues (2025)</ref> raises at least two important take-home messages, depending on how its findings are interpreted.

text.text: On the one hand, when interpreted at face value, the study implies that borderline personality disorder may be more particularly viewed as a self-identity disorder, given that what the authors term as "self-functioning" emerges as the primary aspect of personality that prospectively predicts it.

On the other hand, when interpreted carefully, the study implies that borderline personality disorder may be more accurately viewed as an emotional disorder, given that the authors' predictor measure appears to be saturated with "emotional symptoms" rather than "self-functioning symptoms" (see Table 1).
text.formatted: On the other hand, when interpreted carefully, the study implies that borderline personality disorder may be more accurately viewed as an emotional disorder, given that the authors' predictor measure appears to be saturated with "emotional symptoms" rather than "self-functioning symptoms" (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Either way, the authors' findings cannot support the conclusion that "borderline" kind of difficulties are in any way about "personality" since they can be more specifically viewed to be about primarily one aspect of personality: be it the way one builds an identity or the way one feels inside.

3 Although Sharp and colleagues extend their "borderline-specific" findings to broader "personality pathology" (given the well-replicated finding that borderline symptoms strongly reflect the general "personality disorder" factor), I am reluctant to draw this equivalence because it leads to the logical inference that the general personality factor may actually be an internalising factor (an interpretation that interestingly has some empirical support; Miller et al., 2026 Miller et al., , 2026)).
text.formatted: 3 Although Sharp and colleagues extend their "borderline-specific" findings to broader "personality pathology" (given the well-replicated finding that borderline symptoms strongly reflect the general "personality disorder" factor), I am reluctant to draw this equivalence because it leads to the logical inference that the general personality factor may actually be an internalising factor (an interpretation that interestingly has some empirical support; <ref type="bibr">Miller et al., 2026</ref> <ref type="bibr">Miller et al., , 2026))</ref>.

text.text: Instead, I simply view "borderline" as well as other "personality disorders" in measurement terms: that is, as distinct (though likely overlapping) multi-dimensional measures that emphasise diUerent kinds of symptoms (e.g., just like "borderline" and "personality functioning" measures emphasise internalising symptoms, so could "antisocial" emphasise behavioural symptoms, "schizotypal" cognitive-perceptual symptoms, "dependent" relational symptoms, and so on).

In that sense, all of these "disorders" (or symptoms sets) may ultimately be able to be viewed in more specific terms, leading to the conclusion that there is no such thing as a "personality disorder" as all mental disorders can be understood in more specific terms (e.g., emotional, behavioural, cognitive, or interpersonal disorders; DeYoung & Krueger, 2025; Zavlis & Fonagy, 2024 , 2026).
text.formatted: In that sense, all of these "disorders" (or symptoms sets) may ultimately be able to be viewed in more specific terms, leading to the conclusion that there is no such thing as a "personality disorder" as all mental disorders can be understood in more specific terms (e.g., emotional, behavioural, cognitive, or interpersonal disorders; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">DeYoung & Krueger, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Zavlis & Fonagy, 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: It is important to note that an "identity disorder" is not a "personhood" or a "personality disorder", asSharp et al. (2025, p.19) might infer.
text.formatted: It is important to note that an "identity disorder" is not a "personhood" or a "personality disorder", asSharp et al. (2025, p.19) might infer.

text.text: To elaborate, whileSharp et al. (2025, p.19) equate "personhood" with "an integrated sense of self", the philosophical matter of fact is that "the person" (as a "physical entity"), their personality (as a psychological construct), and their sense of self (as a psychological construct) are distinct objects of inquiry.

Indeed, experts on this topic explicitly distinguish these meanings and caution that "writers should avoid using self as synonym for person and personality in scholarly writing" because a person's self-representation concerns their understanding of themselves, which should not be conflated with "the total person or personality" as a whole (Leary and Tangney, 2012, pp.4-6).

2012, pp.4-6).

text.text: In that sense, an "identity disorder" can be clearly defined as the impairment in how a person views themselves, not an impairment in their personality per se.
text.formatted: In that sense, an "identity disorder" can be clearly defined as the impairment in how a person views themselves, not an impairment in their personality per se.
